title: Projectile Motion with Parametric Equations
short: Model a launched object with x = v₀t cos θ and y = h + v₀t sin θ − 16t².
trouble: Students use the whole launch speed for both the horizontal and the vertical motion.

blocks.html: A ball thrown through the air moves sideways and up-and-down at the same time. Parametric equations let us handle the two motions separately, after splitting the launch velocity into components.

For an object launched at speed $v_0$ ft/s and angle $\theta$ from height $h$ ft (ignoring air resistance): $$x = (v_0\cos\theta)\,t, \qquad y = h + (v_0\sin\theta)\,t - 16t^2.$$ In meters, use $-4.9t^2$. It is highest when $t = \dfrac{v_0\sin\theta}{32}$ and lands when $y = 0$.

The launch velocity is a vector with horizontal part $v_0\cos\theta$ and vertical part $v_0\sin\theta$. Nothing pushes the ball sideways, so the horizontal part stays constant and $x$ grows steadily. Gravity pulls down with acceleration $32$ ft/s², which subtracts $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 32 \cdot t^2 = 16t^2$ from the height. The height is a downward parabola in $t$, so its top is at the vertex, $t = -\frac{b}{2a} = \frac{v_0\sin\theta}{32}$.

blocks.cap: The path stops where the ball lands. The orange and purple arrows are the horizontal and vertical parts of the velocity: the orange one never changes.

blocks.title: From the ground
blocks.q: A ball is kicked from the ground at $64$ ft/s at $30^\circ$. Find its greatest height, when it lands and how far it goes.
steps: Lands when $16t(2 - t) = 0$: $t = 2$ s. Then $x = 64\sqrt{3} \approx 110.9$ ft.
blocks.a: $16$ ft high, lands at $2$ s, about $110.9$ ft away

blocks.title: From a height
blocks.q: A ball is thrown from $6$ ft up at $80\sqrt{2}$ ft/s at $45^\circ$. How high is it after $2$ seconds?

blocks.html: Using the whole launch speed in both equations, such as $x = 64t$ and $y = 64t - 16t^2$. The ball does not move $64$ ft/s sideways and $64$ ft/s up; the speed is split between the two directions by $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$. Check: $(v_0\cos\theta)^2 + (v_0\sin\theta)^2$ should equal $v_0^2$.
